AstroCare is an astronaut health-monitoring and well-being platform designed to support the physical and emotional needs of astronauts during long-duration space missions. Inspired by my fascination with space and my love for poetry and creative writing, I wanted to develop something that looks beyond the technical aspects of space exploration and focuses on the humans behind it.

Built using Python, Streamlit and SQLite, AstroCare brings together Mission Control, Health Lab, Body Explorer, Hazard Zone, Pip Companion, Game Zone and Creative Space. It provides health tracking, educational insights into spaceflight hazards, interactive learning, engagement activities and creative outlets such as journaling, poetry and sharing letters with fellow crew members.

The project addresses the challenge of maintaining astronaut well-being in an isolated and demanding environment. I believe that exploring space should not mean overlooking human emotions. AstroCare represents my attempt to combine technology, science and creativity to make long-duration space missions more human-centred.
details:
ASTROCARE – Crew Health Intelligence
Beyond Survival, Towards Well-being in Space.

When we think about space exploration, we often think about rockets, planets, technology, and how far humans can travel. But one question that interests me just as much is: What happens to the humans making that journey?

This thought became the starting point for AstroCare.

AstroCare is a platform designed around the physical and emotional well-being of astronauts, especially during long-duration space missions. We wanted to create something that looks beyond survival and focuses on the everyday health, comfort, awareness, and well-being of the crew.

Our team brought together three different perspectives. I come from an Automation and Robotics background, while @drtiya is a dental student and @astrolaw is a law student. This made the project especially interesting because we could look at astronaut well-being from different angles: technology, health, and the human and ethical side of space exploration. It reminded us that solving challenges in space is not just an engineering problem; it needs people with different areas of knowledge working together.

The platform brings together seven sections: Mission Control, Health Lab, Body Explorer, Hazard Zone, Creative Corner, Pip Companion, and Game Zone. Through the Health Lab, users can record daily health check-ins and understand changes in their health trends. Body Explorer makes it easier to learn how spaceflight hazards affect the human body, while Hazard Zone introduces the five major human spaceflight hazards. Mission Control brings mission information and crew activities together in one place.

But we didn't want AstroCare to be limited to health charts and technical information. Astronauts on long missions may also experience isolation, stress, and a lack of familiar social environments. That's why we included Creative Corner, where users can write diaries, explore stories, and read poetry. We also added Pip, a friendly rule-based companion, and a Game Zone with activities such as reflex tests, memory games, breathing exercises, and hazard quizzes to make the platform more interactive.

I developed AstroCare using Python, Streamlit, SQLite, HTML, CSS, Pandas, and Plotly. Python handles the main application logic, Streamlit provides the interface, and SQLite is used for data storage. The project is currently a software-based prototype that uses simulated demonstration data and rule-based health insights. It is intended for education and awareness, not as a medical diagnostic tool.

One of my favourite parts of this project is that it brings together two very different interests of mine. As an Automation and Robotics student, I have always been fascinated by space, engineering, and emerging technologies. At the same time, I enjoy poetry and creative writing. I wanted to give both these interests a place in one project. The Creative Corner even includes some of my original poems because I believe that creativity and emotional expression should not become less important just because someone is far away from Earth.

While developing AstroCare, we tried to keep the experience simple, engaging, and easy to understand. We considered the importance of accessible information, personal health tracking, educational value, modular design, and emotional well-being. We also referred to publicly available resources from NASA's Human Research Program and the Canadian Space Agency while developing its educational content.

AstroCare is still a prototype, but the idea behind it is something we genuinely believe in. We wanted to explore how technology and different fields of knowledge could come together to make future space missions more human-centred.

Because exploring space should not only be about how far we can go, but also about how well we can take care of the people who go there.
